title: Acute Flaccid Myelitis Cases Remain Low Despite EV-D68 Respiratory Increases - Infectious Disease Special Edition

analysis.time: Confirmed cases of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) remained low in the United States from 2020 through 2025, despite increases in enterovirus D68 (EV-D68)–associated respiratory illnesses in several years (N1, N17, N18, N19, N24).
analysis.location_and_population: The United States, with a focus on children, as AFM primarily affects them (N8, N9, N22).
analysis.event: Confirmed cases of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) remained low despite increases in EV-D68 respiratory illnesses, and EV-D68 was detected in one AFM specimen in 2025 (N1, N17, N18, N19, N21, N24).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: During 2020 through 2025, confirmed AFM cases ranged from 17 to 48 per year, with a total of 172 cases reported (N19). The CDC noted that increases in EV-D68 respiratory illnesses were not accompanied by concurrent AFM case increases (N24).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC emphasized the importance of continued AFM surveillance and highlighted that viral detection can be limited by specimen collection timing (N22, N26, N27, N33).

analysis.brief_en: This article reports that confirmed cases of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) in the United States remained low from 2020 through 2025, despite increases in enterovirus D68 (EV-D68)–associated respiratory illnesses in 2022, 2024, and 2025. The CDC noted that while EV-D68 was linked to AFM peaks in 2014, 2016, and 2018, the recent years saw no corresponding rise in AFM cases. During the six-year period, 172 confirmed AFM cases were reported, ranging from 17 to 48 annually. Only one AFM specimen tested positive for EV-D68 in 2025. The CDC highlighted the need for continued surveillance due to the similarity of AFM to paralytic poliomyelitis and the limitations in viral detection, particularly when specimens are collected after the onset of symptoms. The findings suggest that EV-D68 circulation does not necessarily lead to AFM cases, and further research is needed to understand this relationship.
analysis.summary_en: This article reports that confirmed cases of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) in the United States remained low from 2020 through 2025, despite increases in enterovirus D68 (EV-D68)–associated respiratory illnesses in 2022, 2024, and 2025. The CDC noted that while EV-D68 was linked to AFM peaks in 2014, 2016, and 2018, the recent years saw no corresponding rise in AFM cases. During the six-year period, 172 confirmed AFM cases were reported, ranging from 17 to 48 annually. Only one AFM specimen tested positive for EV-D68 in 2025. The CDC highlighted the need for continued surveillance due to the similarity of AFM to paralytic poliomyelitis and the limitations in viral detection, particularly when specimens are collected after the onset of symptoms. The findings suggest that EV-D68 circulation does not necessarily lead to AFM cases, and further research is needed to understand this relationship.

title: 3 viruses hit ‘high’ levels in Boise area. See which illnesses are trending

analysis.event: Levels of enterovirus D68, a respiratory virus that can lead to paralysis, remained "high" in Boise's wastewater, according to the WasterWater Scan dashboard. COVID-19 and norovirus have been trending upward in the Boise area for at least 21 days, and both diseases have now reached "high levels" indicating an increase in infections.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Non-polio enteroviruses cause 10 to 15 million infections and tens of thousands of hospitalizations each year in the United States. Infections from EVD68 and other non-polio enteroviruses are most common in the summer and fall, but you can get sick year-round. The virus can be found in an infected person's respiratory secretions, including saliva and mucus. Infections most likely spread through coughs, sneezes and by touching surfaces that have come into contact with those who carry the virus. Severe infections can lead to serious health complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis or meningitis.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare noted that most people with COVID-19 have mild symptoms, but some people can become severely ill resulting in hospitalization or death. Children ages 7 and younger, older adults and people with weakened immune systems are most at risk of developing severe symptoms from viral infections caused by COVID, EVD68 and noroviruses. While there are no known treatments that directly target EVD68 or noroviruses, doctors can attend to some symptoms.

analysis.brief_en: In the Boise area, three viruses—enterovirus D68, COVID-19, and norovirus—are showing high levels in wastewater as of Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Enterovirus D68, a respiratory virus linked to paralysis, has been trending upward for at least 21 days, reaching "high levels" in the region. Similarly, norovirus and SARS-CoV-2 (the virus causing COVID-19) have also reached high concentrations, indicating increased infections. These viruses can cause mild to severe symptoms, including respiratory issues, gastrointestinal problems, and neurological complications like acute flaccid myelitis. The CDC and Mayo Clinic emphasize that while most people may experience mild symptoms, children, older adults, and those with weakened immune systems are at higher risk for severe outcomes. There are no specific vaccines for EVD68 or noroviruses, but antiviral medications and general prevention measures are recommended. Testing is encouraged to help track disease trends and prevent outbreaks.
